data.title: AI in Localization: How to Win, Mitigate Risk, and Capture ROI
What Marketing Executives Need to Know About AI, Automation, and Localization Success

items.heading: Overview
items.text:
Global websites require fast, accurate, and scalable localization across dozens of markets. Often, teams work under tight timelines and with limited internal resources. From product pages and legal disclaimers to SEO content and UX copy, the demand to localize more content, more quickly, keeps growing.
AI is playing a central role in how global organizations approach website localization. Content demands have outpaced traditional workflows, and businesses need ways to localize faster, at scale, and across more languages. AI, particularly in the form of neural machine translation (NMT), offers speed, cost-efficiency, and a level of automation that was out of reach just a few years ago.

items.heading: Key Takeaways
items.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine translation (MT) can help meet that demand—when used strategically. Companies are seeing real gains in speed, scale, and efficiency through AI-powered localization, but the risks are just as real. Poor translation quality, SEO penalties, and compliance issues can quickly erase any benefits.
This guide separates real results from costly missteps. You’ll learn how to:

data.items:
Avoid the most common and expensive mistakes
Combine AI with human expertise for better results
Build a scalable localization strategy that protects your brand

data.title: We’ll also look ahead to what’s coming next—so you can prepare now for the future of AI in global content.

SECTION 1 - INTRODUCTION: AI & Website Localization in 2025: The Opportunity & Risks — Why AI-driven localization is a game-changer—but only if done right.
SECTION 2: The Wins: What’s Working in AI-Powered Localizations — How AI and automation are helping businesses scale localization faster and more efficiently.
SECTION 3: The Risks – Hidden Pitfalls that Harm AI Localization Efforts — The real cost of poor AI localization—and how businesses can avoid disaster.
SECTION 4: Turning Insights into Action: How to Build a Smarter AI Localization Strategy — Building an AI-Powered Localization Strategy That Works
SECTION 5 – CONCLUSION: Future-Proofing Your Website Localization Strategy

items.heading: SECTION 1 - INTRODUCTION: AI & Website Localization in 2025: The Opportunity & Risks
items.text: Why AI-driven localization is a game-changer—but only if done right.

But AI is not a strategy on its own. As adoption accelerates, the gap is widening between companies that deploy it strategically—and those that deploy it carelessly. What we’re seeing now is a shift from experimentation to operationalization, where the stakes are much higher.

items.heading: Opportunities
items.text:
When used effectively, AI enables businesses to localize more content, across more languages, with less manual effort. Content like support articles, product descriptions, or seasonal campaigns can be processed in hours rather than days or weeks. This kind of throughput is critical for keeping up with modern digital marketing demands.

In the right conditions, machine translation quality has improved significantly, especially in high-resource languages like Spanish, French, and German. Teams that integrate AI into a structured localization workflow, using post-editing or review tiers based on content type and risk level, are seeing real wins in speed, budget efficiency, and time to market.

AI also allows for faster go-to-market testing and expansion. Brands can pilot new locales quickly, validate market interest, and scale successful launches without overcommitting upfront resources.

items.heading: Risks
items.text:
The biggest risks come when AI is treated as a standalone solution. Machine translation alone cannot account for cultural nuance, brand tone, legal requirements, or SEO strategy. In some cases, it can even create active harm—damaging brand credibility, misinforming users, or violating regulatory standards.

Even technically, there are hazards: Without clear source content, proper CMS integration, and localization QA, AI-generated translations can create broken experiences and block content from search engine indexing.

items.heading: Purpose of This Guide
items.text:
This guide is built to help you navigate the real-world use of AI in website localization. You’ll find clarity on where AI delivers, where it doesn’t, and how to structure your workflows to balance quality, scale, and cost.

Whether you’re exploring AI and localization for the first time or scaling an established program, this resource is here to help you avoid the most common mistakes, take advantage of proven best practices, and prepare your team for what’s coming next.

items.heading: SECTION 2: The Wins – What’s Working in Website Localization Today
items.text: How AI is helping businesses scale localization faster.

items.heading: 2.1 Accelerating Content Localization
items.text: AI-powered machine translation dramatically shortens the localization process, helping global brands launch multilingual content rapidly. Compared to traditional workflows that often require weeks of human-driven translations, AI can produce quality translations almost instantly—making multilingual launches faster than ever.

items.heading: Scale Effortlessly & Efficiently
items.text:
Manual localization processes slow global growth. AI-driven automation eliminates repetitive tasks like manual submissions and overly tedious approvals, freeing your teams to focus on higher-impact, strategic localization decisions.

Benefits at a glance:
items.bullets:
Speed: Reduce localization timelines dramatically
Efficiency: Eliminate administrative overhead
Scalability: Easily expand into new markets and languages

items.heading: Real-World Examples of AI Localization Success
items.text: Leading global brands are already using AI and automation to achieve measurable business wins:

items.heading: Retail: AI Makes 1M+ Product Launches Feasible
items.text: A major eCommerce retailer with over 1 million SKUs used AI to localize their entire catalog—a feat that would have been impossible with manual translation due to cost. AI allowed them to enter multiple new markets quickly and cost-effectively, with human review layered in for high-priority content. This strategy removed a key go-to-market barrier.

items.heading: Hospitality: Scaling Hotel Content in 20+ Languages
items.text: A leading global hospitality brand used machine translation to achieve content parity with their English website. Previously, only select property pages were translated. After onboarding with customized MT engines and regional stakeholder buy-in, they scaled to translate thousands of hotel descriptions, booking flows, and property content into over 20 languages. This shift enabled a fully multilingual user experience across their portfolio—without the resource drain of human-only translation.

items.heading: Life Sciences: Speeding Up Patient Recruitment
items.text: In the clinical research space, one pharmaceutical company used AI to localize patient recruitment content across multiple geographies under a tight deadline. By combining GlobalLink Web with AI-powered workflows, they accelerated patient enrollment for global trials while meeting strict regulatory and accuracy requirement.

items.heading: 2.2 When does AI Work? When Are Humans Essential?
items.text: Not all localization tasks are created equal. Content types that are straightforward and high in volume like product descriptions or standard FAQs are ideal candidates for AI-driven translation, offering speed and consistency at scale. But nuanced or sensitive content such as legal documents, compliance-driven materials, or brand-critical messaging should always involve human linguists to ensure cultural accuracy, compliance, and brand consistency.

items.heading: Hybrid Approach: Combining AI Speed and Human Precision
items.text: The best localization strategies adopt a hybrid model, blending AI-generated translations with human oversight. This method delivers optimal balance between efficiency, scalability, and quality. A typical hybrid workflow might look like:
items.bullets:
AI Translation First: Quickly generates a baseline translation for review.
Human Validation Second: Linguists refine translations, ensuring accuracy, cultural appropriateness, and compliance.

items.heading: Hybrid Success Example: Multinational Tech Brand
items.text: One multinational technology provider implemented a hybrid AI-human workflow using GlobalLink Web. They used AI to instantly translate support content into 15 languages, then added human review for UX strings, regulatory language, and brand voice. The result? A 40% reduction in time-to-market for new feature launches and improved international customer satisfaction scores within six months.

data.title: 2.3 The Rise of Adaptive Content & Personalization

items.heading: Market-Specific Messaging: Why AI Personalization Matters
items.text: Customers expect relevant, culturally appropriate messaging—something generic translations can’t provide. AI makes it easier to tailor messaging by quickly generating localized content drafts that marketing and localization experts can adapt for specific market nuances and customer preferences.

items.heading: The Engagement Advantage
items.text: Brands that deliver personalized experiences through localized content significantly outperform generic translations. Localized content fosters trust, builds stronger emotional connections, and drives higher conversion rates across global audiences.

items.heading: Flexible Approaches: AI Drafts, Expert Refinement
items.text: Successful brands use AI strategically to accelerate localization at scale, then empower human experts to finalize content. This approach ensures both personalization and brand authenticity.

items.heading: Every Language Requires Its Own Strategy
items.text: Languages differ vastly in complexity, cultural nuances, and localization challenges. For example, AI may perform exceptionally well for straightforward languages like Spanish or German but struggle with more structurally complex languages like Japanese or Arabic, where human oversight becomes critical.

items.heading: Content Type Matters
items.text: Content complexity directly influences AI effectiveness. Transactional content such as product listings or help-center articles can usually rely heavily on automation. But creative, compliance-driven, or brand-sensitive content needs strategic human review to maintain quality and mitigate risks.
items.bullets:
Low Complexity (Highly Automated): FAQs, product specs, basic web content.
High Complexity (Human Validation Critical): Legal, compliance, UX/UI, marketing copy.

items.heading: Improving Accuracy with Pre-Trained Models
items.text: AI translation quality heavily depends on the quality of pre-trained translation models. Continuously training these models on industry-specific terms, brand-specific voice, and customer feedback can greatly enhance translation accuracy and reduce the need for extensive human editing.

The most successful localization strategies harness the strengths of both AI and human expertise. AI offers speed and scalability, while human linguists provide cultural insight, brand alignment, and precision. Together, this hybrid approach delivers faster time-to-market, consistent quality, and greater confidence as you grow globally.

items.heading: SECTION 3: The Risks – Hidden Pitfalls that Harm AI Localization Efforts
items.text: The real cost of poor AI localization—and how businesses can avoid disaster

items.heading: 3.1 Overestimating AI: Why Automation Alone Won’t Work
items.text: As AI becomes more accessible, many businesses rush to implement it without a clear understanding of its limitations. The assumption that automation can handle all aspects of localization—across all content types, languages, and regulatory environments—often leads to costly missteps. AI is a tool, not a strategy, and using it effectively requires knowing when to rely on automation and when human oversight is non-negotiable.

items.heading: Myth: AI-powered CMS solutions solve everything
items.text:
AI offers powerful localization capabilities, but treating it as a plug-and-play solution inevitably leads to failure. Businesses often assume automation will flawlessly handle complex content, compliance details, and nuanced language differences, which—at this point—simply isn’t realistic.

Common AI localization mistakes:
items.bullets:
Skipping human validation: Fully automated workflows often result in culturally inappropriate translations and errors in critical content.
Ignoring content complexity: Not all content types benefit equally from AI. Assuming otherwise creates costly and brand-damaging quality issues.

items.heading: The Turkey Mistake
items.text: A brand allowed untranslated content to go live using fully automated workflows. The result? “Made in Turkey” became “Made in Turkey (the bird)”—a clear sign of machine translation without context. Errors like these erode trust and become memes.

items.heading: “Home” Mistranslated in UI
items.text: In a German navigation menu, the word “Home” was translated as “zu Hause” (as in one’s house) rather than “Startseite” (home page). This context mismatch confused users and showed the risks of translating UI elements without human oversight.

items.heading: 3.2 SEO & Multilingual Website Challenges
items.text: AI-generated translations can pose real risks to your SEO performance. When not carefully reviewed, they can result in low-quality content that’s duplicated, too thin to be valuable, or contextually irrelevant—factors that can trigger search engine penalties from platforms like Google.

data.title: Avoid SEO penalties with a smarter strategy

items.title: Quality-first approach
items.text: Prioritize human review to ensure every translation is relevant, accurate, and aligned with your keyword strategy.

items.title: Structured oversight
items.text: Use AI for scale, but pair it with human SEO expertise to safeguard and strengthen your visibility in global markets.

items.title: Tracking the ROI of Multilingual SEO
items.text: Monitor organic rankings, website traffic, and engagement across languages to evaluate the real impact of high-quality, SEO-driven localization.

items.heading: 3.3 Localized UX/UI Challenges
items.text: AI often falls short when it comes to translating UI labels and capturing contextual nuance. Without an understanding of how text functions within a user interface, automated translations can produce confusing or misleading buttons, menus, and navigation elements.

items.heading: Cultural nuances directly impact usability
items.text: When UI translations are inconsistent or unclear, users get frustrated. This leads to lower engagement, higher bounce rates, and a decline in user trust, particularly in unfamiliar markets.

items.heading: Why getting UI translations right matters
items.text: A poorly localized interface doesn’t just feel clunky, it can severely damage your brand’s credibility and hurt long-term success in global markets.

items.heading: Overview
items.text: The Retail Hive has produced this report in collaboration with TransPerfect, using both qualitative and quantitative research methods to ensure a deep dive into the opportunities and challenges surrounding global e-commerce.

items.heading: Research Methodology and Demographics
items.text:
The Retail Hive has produced this report in collaboration with TransPerfect, using both qualitative and quantitative research methods to ensure a deep dive into the opportunities and challenges surrounding global e-commerce.

The statistics in this report are based on an industry survey of 31 international leaders, conducted in Q2 and Q3 of 2023, and supported by interviews and insights from a hand-picked group of retail experts at varying stages of their global e-commerce journey.

items.heading: Contributing Brands
items.text: As always, a huge thank you to our contributors and members for their continued insights and expertise.

items.heading: Opening Remarks from TransPerfect
items.text:
The retail world is rapidly changing and challenging at the best of times, but in the last five years, it has gone through some existential challenges—from COVID-19 closing down the vast majority of brick-and-mortar organizations and the shift to online buying habits to shipping delays, inflation and legislative changes, such as Brexit for European retailers and changing technical architectures.

It is no surprise a lot of brands feel like they have been treading water, keeping their head above the crashing waves of the last challenge, only to see another one on the horizon building pace towards them. However, as some of these challenges begin to settle and the water becomes a little calmer, the focus has shifted back to growth and expansion.

With many home markets slowing down and 74% of retailers in this report saying growth is the focus for 2024, international is the prominent place to look. Cross-border is continuing to grow, making up 22% of e-commerce shipments, amounting to more than $3.5 trillion. However, with this tempting opportunity, it is important to go in with eyes wide open. Global e-commerce is a Pandora’s box—first, there are logistics, tariff and tax conversions, followed by the ability to take local payments, quick returns and then localizing and translating this offering to each market.

There is also increasing pressure to ensure brands are localizing authentically and understanding how these international markets live and shop vs. copying and pasting a home strategy. There is a large ecosystem of suppliers and partnerships that work together to ensure the challenges of cross-border are not insurmountable—from local knowledge to AI tools and the options of build, buy and partner.

This study looks to benchmark the current mood of international, along with the challenges, opportunities, building blocks, and advice of retailers currently on this journey.

Aaron Campbell, Director, UK Retail, TransPerfect

items.heading: The Appetite for International Expansion
items.text:
International expansion is a key area of growth for Retail Hive members. In 2024, 26% of brands surveyed have a significant target for growth, targeting over 50% of business coming from non-domestic markets. After years of rapid gains, e-commerce growth in the UK and US is leveling out, staying relatively consistent in both markets at around 4% growth year-on-year—a similar rate to that of brick-and-mortar sales. So, it is no surprise to learn that retailers wanting bigger growth opportunities are looking to countries where e-commerce saturation is not as profound.

Currently, 29% of members/survey respondents have just 1-10% of business coming from abroad, while 39% of this group have over 26% of business taking place in other countries. There is clearly an appetite for international expansion among brands, but just how much of a strategic priority is global e-commerce?

items.heading: Pipped to The Post: Prioritizing International Expansion
items.text:
74% of members see global e-commerce as one of their top priorities. Delving deeper into these numbers, we discover that 58% of retailers regard global e-commerce as one of their ‘Top 3’ or ‘Top 5’ strategic priorities. However, while international expansion continues to be a top priority for many brands, it is seldom a ‘Number 1’ priority, with just 16% of members giving it top spot.

From TransPerfect’s perspective, the e-commerce arena is a battleground of conflicting and changing priorities. It has such a broad depth that there is always something “on fire” that takes the ‘Number 1’ priority, and naturally, decisions are made on what will impact the dominant/home markets. It is, therefore, no surprise that global e-commerce is always in the ‘Top 5’, but rarely ‘Number 1’. The aspiration is often there, but brands need some support and guidance on how to do this most effectively, proving the effort’s ROI at multiple stages. Senior leadership buy-in to alleviate some of these concerns is key.

items.heading: How High on Your List of Strategic Priorities is Global E-Commerce?
items.text: Of those surveyed, only 19% are pulling back on international investment or not prioritizing this at all.
items.bullets:
Number 1: 16%
Top 3: 29%
Top 5: 29%
Not a Priority: 13%
Pulling Back on Investment: 6%
Other: 7%

items.heading: Global e-commerce is often considered a ‘Top 5’ priority, but rarely ‘Number 1’. Does this surprise you?
items.text:
“No, it doesn’t surprise me at all. When looking at domestic growth vs. international growth, international growth is more complex. However, I’m not surprised that more and more people are doing it; if you’re sitting in the UK, the general economic outlook is negative for a lot of retailers at different levels. It’s about strategic choices of growth—product, service price—and within that, markets/channels.

Interestingly, in some of the businesses I’ve worked in, we decided that we wanted to take more market share in the UK, become more price competitive and improve our service proposition as a route to growth. In another business, which was private equity, the only way to increase the value of the business was to get some international, proven credibility for the brand.”

Simon Ratcliffe — Seasoned Supply Chain and Logistics Director, Various Companies (The Just Group (AUS), Debenhams)

items.heading: Current and Target Countries
items.text:
In terms of country focus, native English-speaking countries (i.e. the UK, USA, Canada and Australia) score highly on current international markets, perhaps because it is relatively easy for brands to extend their e-commerce offering to countries with cultural and linguistic similarities.

In which of the following countries are you active/exploring? Current, or priority for the next 12 months?

When looking at the location of survey respondents, it also becomes clear that members have selected neighboring countries within central locations, maintaining close proximity to their current customers and suppliers. For example, most respondents in the US selected Canada and Latin America as their current and target areas, whereas the majority of UK respondents opted for France and Germany.

items.heading: Outside of convenient location, TransPerfect see a couple of other main points when brands are looking at new markets, including
items.bullets:
Demographics of the market
Market growth rate
Forecasted demand - i.e. for a maternity brand, which markets have high birth rates?
Competitors already in the market
Potential barriers to entry – language, fulfilment, payments etc.
Average return rates per market

items.text:
Over the next year, Germany, France and Mediterranean Europe are high on the list of new markets to enter. E-commerce saturation in these markets compared to the US and UK leaves plenty of room for growth. China also represents a sizable opportunity in terms of the number of consumers shopping online and appetite for Western brands, but tapping into China is no easy feat.

In TransPerfect’s view, China has incredible potential, but it’s a tightrope—from strict advertising rules (no superlatives like “superior” or “the best”) to considerations on Chinese sovereignty (be careful on flag selection), not to mention the predominant route of marketplace vs. build for most western brands and the cultural challenges these partnerships might involve.

items.heading: People, Resource and Expertise
items.text:
‘Clunky logistics and warehousing’ was ranked the biggest hindrance to digital growth by brands. This is unsurprising given that many members of The Retail Hive’s fulfilment and supply chain community have spent the past year grappling with the difficulty of integrating new, state-of-the-art technologies with legacy warehouse systems. In the UK, logistics challenges are also compounded by ongoing issues with Brexit.

The top two blockers for cross-border e-commerce—i.e. pressure on resource and operations—can be mitigated by automation and AI, which are set to supercharge all areas of the retail industry.

items.heading: Jo Hickson, Head of Technology and Group Innovation, Tesco
items.text: “Generative AI isn’t a part of the future, it’s a step change. As a team, we’re currently looking at the practical applications of generative AI for the business. For example, by the end of next year, if you’re a Microsoft house and you’re using Outlook, you’ll have their AI assistant to help you do your job better. There’s nowhere it’s not going to have an effect.”

items.heading: Stuart Ramage, Head of Digital Strategy, Marks and Spencer
items.text: “By the back end of 2024, there’ll be an explosion of retailers with the ability to truly connect all their assets—from stores to warehouses, trucks, colleagues and customers. This will be true omnichannel capabilities, at scale, driven by automation.”

Members selected ‘lack of resource’ as the second biggest hindrance to digital growth. In our survey, ‘resourcing’ encompasses three core areas: lack of resource, local market expertise, and having the right partners in place. Ultimately, this comes down to who in the business owns the international strategy, working effectively with international sites, marketing teams and partners to generate sales and drive loyalty.

‘Not working with the right partners’ is considered the third biggest hindrance to overseas growth. Arguably, all three of these factors are inextricably linked—having the right partners in place enables much smoother technology integration, and the adoption of AI and automated tools relieves workers of repetitive, manual tasks and boosts overall efficiency, helping to solve the resourcing issue. Retailers shouldn’t underestimate the power of people, resource and expertise when it comes to digital growth.

items.heading: How do you select partners?
items.text:
“They need to be the right cultural fit—having that sense of purpose and being passionate about the same things as us is really important. The Body Shop is a triple bottom line business, so we really want to drive positive change in the world, and we’re so excited and passionate about driving that change. Commercially, it needs to work for us and for them. Also having a local partner who really understands how to manage business in those markets makes a huge difference.”

Hilary McNair — International Head Franchise Commercial and Digital Director, The Body Shop

items.heading: Do you need a partner for international growth?
items.text:
“It depends how big you are and how much cash you’ve got. There’s that tradeoff between doing it on your own and controlling it—which is probably more complex—or going with a partner, where you’ll probably have margin dilution because you’re sharing it with your partner, but you can get into the market much faster and they’ll know it better than you. That trade-off is a really interesting, board-level discussion.”

Simon Ratcliffe — Seasoned Supply Chain and Logistics Director, Various Companies (The Just Group (AUS), Debenhams)

data.title: Pieces to the Puzzle: International Strategy Components
data.intro: As for international strategy components, ‘D2C through own localized site’ received the highest number of votes from members. A close second was ‘wholesale’, with ‘marketplaces’ and ‘stores’ coming joint third.

items.heading: Do you enter markets with a physical-first or digital-first approach?
items.text:
“Normally, we’ll go in with a physical footprint first. This is the best experience for our brand, particularly for a category like beauty products; your best experience is being able to touch and play with the products, and it’s sometimes difficult to get a sense of that online. You can get this across much better in store.”

Hilary McNair — International Head Franchise Commercial and Digital Director, The Body Shop

data.title: Your Multilingual SEO Success Checklist: 5 Essential Steps for Enterprises

items.heading: Overview
items.text: Multilingual SEO isn't just about translating content — it's about ensuring discoverability, cultural relevance, and technical optimization in every market. Use this checklist to streamline your strategy and drive organic traffic in target regions.

items.heading: 1–2. Identify and refine keywords
items.text: Conduct keyword research in both source and target languages, then refine for cultural preference and local terminology rather than translating terms literally.
items.bullets:
Align keywords with local search behavior and user intent
Use Google Keyword Planner, Semrush, or Ahrefs for high-impact terms
Collaborate with native speakers or linguists; verify in local engines

items.heading: What Is Localization?
items.text: Localization is the process of adapting content, design, and multimedia to be linguistically and culturally appropriate for global audiences. This goes beyond translation—it’s also about tailoring visuals and layouts to align with the cultural norms and preferences of each market. For instance, an image of a car on a U.S. website might need to be replaced with one showing the steering wheel on the right side for regions where that is the norm.

items.heading: Benefits of Localization
items.text: Understanding the advantages of localization can help you connect with global audiences in a more meaningful way. A few benefits of localization include:
items.bullets:
Wider market reach—Your potential customer base will expand significantly across diverse regions.
Better user experience—Website visitors will not struggle to understand or relate to your content, making it easier to complete transactions.
Brand loyalty and trust—Localized websites demonstrate that your organization values cultural diversity and is dedicated to delivering a customer experience that feels natural and tailored to each audience.
Competitive advantage—You will gain an edge over competitors who have not localized their websites or have limited their localization to fewer markets.

data.title: Achieving these benefits can feel like a daunting task. However, advances in technology have made localization more feasible than ever before.

items.heading: AI + Humans: A Hybrid Approach
items.text: Today’s leading organizations utilize a blend of AI and human expertise to scale their localization efforts efficiently. While AI brings significant advancements and streamlines many aspects of the process, a hybrid AI-human approach ensures that every detail is handled with precision. Human linguists provide critical oversight to deliver:
items.bullets:
Accuracy in translated content
Cultural relevance and sensitivity
Appropriate, natural tone
Consistent brand voice
Correct use of terminology—which is especially important in complex, technical content
Compliance with local regulations

items.heading: What Website Elements Should Be Localized?
items.text: To create a seamless experience for local audiences, your website should be adapted to feel native to local audiences. Key elements to consider include:
items.bullets:
Dialects and spellings
Colors
Images, icons, and symbols
Local units of measure and currency
Date and time formats
Page layout
Idioms, humor, and cultural references
Local laws and regulations

items.heading: Localizing Your Website? Here’s What You Need To Know.
items.text:
Expanding your business into global markets brings exciting opportunities and a long to-do list. You know you will need multiple language versions of your website, but you may not be aware of everything this entails. Localizing your website requires both linguistic and cultural adaptations, with various near-term and ongoing considerations. Whether you are in the planning stages or are ready to work with a language services provider and translation management system to handle the process, it is helpful to understand what is ahead.

Here are ten important considerations for localizing your website:

items.heading: Know Your Audiences
items.text: Suppose you have decided to expand into several European markets. Your source website will need to be localized for each country in which you plan to grow your business. An in-depth understanding of your target customers’ cultural norms and preferences is essential in determining which aspects of your site require localization. Visually, this might include colors, imagery, and layout. In terms of content, localization goes beyond translation and may entail adjustments to humor, idioms, and regional references.

items.heading: Localize All Content
items.text: Which parts of your website should be localized? The answer is all of it—even the parts that are not immediately visible to users. Here are some elements to consider:

items.title: Written content
items.text: Body copy, keywords, and any text in graphics and videos. Adjust idioms, cultural references, units of measure, currencies, and date and time formats.

items.title: Visuals
items.text: Photos, graphics, and videos, all of which should reflect cultural preferences.

items.title: Unseen text
items.text: Metadata, alt text, and hreflang tags, all of which are important for accessibility and SEO.

items.heading: Style Guide & Glossary
items.text: It is good practice to create a style guide and glossary to maintain consistency across your localized websites. A style guide outlines the rules for content creation, while a glossary provides definitions and preferred translations for key terms. These tools ensure your localized sites reflect your brand image and voice.

items.heading: Local Keywords and International SEO
items.text: Your website should be just as discoverable by users in other languages and markets as it is by for your native audience. It’s important to understand how people in your target markets search for the products and services your company offers. You will need a tailored SEO approach for each language you are targeting. This includes integrating local keywords into your site content to boost visibility and building backlinks from other local businesses in your target markets.

items.heading: Legal and Regulatory Compliance
items.text: When localizing your website for other countries, you must be mindful of regulations and laws in each region. This includes laws and guidelines regarding data collection and usage, privacy, copyright and IP laws, consumer protection, and accessibility. Failing to adhere to these regulations can result in significant consequences, including fines and lost trust with local audiences.

items.heading: Cultural Relevance
items.text: For localization to be effective, it must consider cultural nuances. For example, while the phrase “As American as apple pie” may be common in the U.S., its literal translation may not mean anything to non-English speakers. Similarly, using U.S. sizes for clothing, U.S. currency for pricing, or images of American celebrities may need to be adjusted for different markets to remain culturally relevant.

items.heading: QA Testing
items.text: Thorough quality assurance testing is a vital part of website localization. This ensures that translated content retains its intended meaning and adheres to cultural conventions. It also involves verifying that links, forms, and buttons work properly on localized sites and that the user interface and experience resonate with local audiences and on various devices and browsers. Additionally, translations can alter the length of text, so it is important to check for any cut-off or misaligned text.

items.heading: Local Expertise
items.text: Collaborating with local marketing experts or cultural consultants can help you tailor your website and content strategy for specific audiences. These experts can keep you updated on industry trends and cultural shifts, keeping your localization efforts relevant within your target markets.

items.heading: Choose the Right Tool
items.text:
Managing multilingual websites can be labor-intensive. At a minimum, you will need a translator, developer, graphic designer, and QA engineer. However, your company may not have the internal resources to devote to the ongoing task of managing localized websites. A Translation Management System (TMS) centralizes management and streamlines the website localization process, alleviating the burden on your internal teams while increasing content consistency, accuracy, and quality. A TMS combines machine translation, translation memory, and workflow management features in a single platform.

With a TMS, any updates to your source site will be automatically detected and carried through to your localized sites. This ensures consistency and coherence across markets and reduces the risk of outdated or misaligned content. Additionally, the TMS will store previously translated content in translation memory to prevent duplicate translations later on. For instance, you might make updates to your source site that need to be reflected on your Spanish, French, and Chinese sites. In that case, your TMS would draw on previously translated content in the translation memory, only performing new translations as needed.

items.heading: Benefits of Using a Translation Management System
items.bullets:
Lower cost for translations and multisite management
Increased localization efficiency
Consistency in translations
Tight coordination between AI-powered machine translation and human review

items.heading: Final Thoughts
items.text:
Website localization is crucial for expanding your company’s reach beyond domestic markets. Speaking the local languages of your global customers fosters trust and loyalty. A skillfully localized site makes it easier for prospective customers to find you, navigate your site, and complete purchases. Localization also contributes to brand satisfaction and loyalty, as your site will feel intuitive and natural to customers in non-local markets and will increase the likelihood of new and repeat business. A translation management system that integrates with your existing systems maximizes the efficiency of the entire localization process.

items.heading: The Solution
items.text: Whether you intend to use machine translation (MT) to simply understand a document in another language or in conjunction with post-editing for a high-quality end product, our diverse array of MT services offer different quality levels to adapt to any business need.

items.heading: Raw MT
items.text: Pure MT output with no human editing produced by one of our off-the-shelf MT solutions, including our industry domain engines. This is MT that does not take terminology or style into account and that is typically employed for “gisting” or understandability purposes.

items.heading: Customized MT
items.text: Pure MT output with no human editing produced by MT engines customized with client assets such as terminology and translation memories (TM). This type of MT yields improved accuracy and higher quality in comparison to our off-the-shelf solutions and is highly recommended for any scenario in which MT is used without human editing.

items.heading: Light-Post Editing
items.text: Understandable translation with no major errors but that is not stylistically perfect, and is ideal for lower-priority content where speed is more important than quality.

items.heading: Full-Post Editing
items.text: Top-tier translation that is equivalent to the quality expected of a standard human translation process. While not recommended for very creative texts, this service is ideal for high-visibility, customer-facing content and is intended to be indistinguishable from a human translation.

data.title: GlobalLink & PIM: How to Efficiently Manage Your Brand's
data.short: GlobalLink & PIM: How to Efficiently Manage Your Brand's

items.heading: The Solution
items.text: Anyone making an online purchase, whether it's a physical product or a digital service, is at a disadvantage for a few reasons. A consumer can't test or feel a physical product ahead of time. Similarly, for a digital service, consumers can't experience it until after they buy it. So how can they confidently make the purchase and know that they are buying the right thing? By having the most accurate, comprehensive information about the product to educate themselves. And how can organizations selling or marketing these products arm their consumers with the best information? With a product information management (PIM) platform.

items.heading: The Single Source of Truth for All Product Information
items.text: A product information management (PIM) system acts as a central platform to collect, manage, govern, and enrich product information and content and distribute it to marketing, sales, and e-commerce channels. Brands typically utilize a PIM in a single database application to store product portfolio information such as images, datasheets, and videos. A PIM system also helps you control product presentation, ensuring consistency across all available channels and reinforcing your brand story. Simply put, any organization that is driven by e-commerce cannot operate without a PIM strategy.

items.heading: Enhance Your MarTech Stack with a PIM
items.text: Your MarTech stack consists of many technologies, everything from a CMS to CRM, that enable your team to optimize their marketing initiatives. And while is it critical to have a robust martech stack, having the right PIM platform is equally important for ensuring success across every division of your organization.
items.bullets:
Provide all the necessary information to the seller or customer to guide them in the sale or purchase of a product.
Manage data required to create any marketing content, from catalogs to PDFs, throughout the sales process.

items.heading: The Benefits of a PIM
items.text: Delivering engaging product experiences is a crucial success factor for your business-whether it's B2B or B2C. Customers expect to see the correct information across all of your channels and digital touchpoints when making informed decisions about their purchases. If product information is either incomplete or inconsistent across channels, internal teams do not receive the full scope of the product. This can lead to missed opportunities, loss of revenue, and negative customer experiences.

items.heading: Top 5 Benefits
items.bullets:
Faster time-to-market
Increased brand loyalty
Ability to sell more products, faster
Improved operational efficiencies by streamlining critical workflows and cross-functional collaborative data enrichment
More engaging, omnichannel product experience

items.text: Strong translation and localization methods help organizations easily and efficiently launch and maintain multilingual product information. GlobalLink can seamlessly integrate into PIM solutions, providing better translation experiences for clients and easy-to-use translation management interfaces. It's important to localize product content for your target audience. It's also imperative to create a compelling and trusting connection with consumers, which then generates high levels of customer loyalty. A reliable TMS paired with a PIM can create a universally positive customer service experience. By leveraging the power of GlobalLink and a PIM, your organization can:

The system also permits translators to reuse parts of translated phrases, speeding up the translation process while decreasing costs.

data.title: What Enterprise Retail Teams Should Validate Before Shortlisting a TMS

items.heading: Overview
items.text: Use this checklist to align Marketing, Digital, IT, and Procurement on what matters most when evaluating localization platforms for retail and consumer goods.

items.heading: 1. Retail Architecture Fit
items.text: Can the TMS work with how your retail systems actually operate?
items.bullets:
Does it integrate natively with your PIM, CMS, and e-commerce platforms?
Can it handle structured product data, not just flat content?
Does it support multi-brand and multi-site environments?
Why this matters: Retail content lives across systems. Manual handoffs introduce risk and delay.

items.heading: 2. SKU Velocity & Content Change
items.text: Can the platform keep up with retail's pace of change?
items.bullets:
Can it localize thousands of SKUs at once?
Does it support frequent updates for promotions, pricing, and seasonal changes?
Can attributes, metadata, and variants flow automatically?
Why this matters: Retail localization is never “done.” Speed and repeatability are critical.

items.heading: 3. AI Use with Control
items.text: Is AI applied responsibly and measurably?
items.bullets:
Can different content types use different AI models or workflows?
Is human review available where accuracy or compliance matters?
Can quality be measured and reviewed, not just assumed?
Why this matters: Retail teams need AI that scales output without increasing risk.

items.heading: 4. Omnichannel Quality & Performance
items.text: Does localized content perform across every channel?
items.bullets:
Is SEO and metadata localization supported by market?
Can content stay consistent across PDPs, marketplaces, and apps?
Is brand tone and terminology enforced centrally?
Why this matters: Translation quality alone does not guarantee conversion or trust.

items.heading: 5. Governance, Security & Compliance
items.text: Is the platform enterprise-ready?
items.bullets:
Does it meet enterprise security and compliance standards?
Are audit trails and approvals built in?
Can access and permissions be controlled across teams and regions?
Why this matters: Retail brands carry regulatory, reputational, and operational risk.

items.heading: 6. Scalability & Expertise
items.text: Will this solution scale with your business?
items.bullets:
Can it support global growth without adding operational overhead?
Is retail and CPG expertise available beyond the software?
Does the provider offer guidance on workflows and governance?

items.heading: The Challenge
items.text: Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E) had developed a collection of digital learning courses with another vendor for PG&E's ESA Program, but they were dissatisfied with the outcomes. The courses lacked engagement, and the translations were low-quality, putting the success of the ESA at risk.

items.heading: The Solution
items.text: Given the poor engagement and negative feedback from their Spanish markets, PG&E sought a vendor for content updates. Initially, they wanted to make minor edits to a couple of sections within one of the courses. However, after speaking with TransPerfect Learning Solutions, PG&E decided to partner with them to better the learner experience and align the Spanish content with the elevated English versions. TransPerfect's instructional design experts identified some key areas of concern, which lacked engagement. To combat this and to work efficiently, they implemented "quick wins" opportunities. This included chunking information, creating interactions, and enhancing visuals, among other methods. Each course was also updated to ensure it met the current California Installation Standards Manual to avoid any discrepancies across assets.

items.heading: The Result
items.text: PG&E's top priority is to provide engaging digital content that creates measurable behavior change. To address these objectives, TransPerfect Learning Solutions collaborated with a former PG&E employee, who served as a subject matter expert. This partnership resulted in a streamlined content review process, reducing client review time and ensuring accurate content changes to meet all compliance requirements in 2023.
items.bullets:
TransPerfect doubled PG&E's course output from 8 to 16, accommodating a total of 367 students.
The Net Promoter Score (NPS) experienced significant growth, rising from 56.25 to 74.68 in Q4, surpassing the initial target of 50%.
TransPerfect created an automation strategy to deliver impactful training using a unique automated speech program that captures exclusive acronyms and industry-specific terminology, ensuring authentic training without relying solely on human voice actors.

items.caption: Customer pass rate across collection and annotation
Segmentations delivered. Polygons and bounding boxes
Attributes captured. Up to eight per bottle
Time to delivery. Full collection to delivery

items.heading: Overview
items.text: A custom photo-collection and segmentation pipeline that gave an intelligent inventory startup the high-quality training data its shelf-monitoring model needed.

items.heading: The challenge
items.text: Aapya Solutions built Eyes on Shelves, an intelligent inventory system powered by its proprietary Vision-37 Inventory Intelligence Platform. Retailers struggle daily with inventory accuracy, real-time shelf visibility, product loss, and planogram compliance — and manual shelf audits are expensive. Aapya needed a partner to accelerate turnaround and collect high-quality data to train its model for 24/7/365 shelf monitoring, while protecting customer data as an emerging startup.

items.heading: Our solution
items.text: DataForce built a custom data collection pipeline and QA process near Aapya's Tampa Bay headquarters, sourcing a local community member to photograph 300+ liquor products and their barcodes over three days. Photos flowed straight into our cloud through DataForce Contribute, our mobile app. Scope covered aisle-segment and individual bottle photos, up to eight attributes per bottle, and segmentation of every bottle (polygons) and barcode (bounding boxes). A three-coordinate workflow — aisle segment, shelf number, position on shelf — let attributes be entered once and transposed across photo types, cutting collection and annotation time and cost. Our technology team scripted the attribute transposition and generated YOLOv8 format output, a first for DataForce.

items.heading: The result
items.text: Six aisle-segment photos and 350 individual bottle photos produced 356 photos, 2,800 attributes, and 700 segmentations, plus an additional 468 segmentations and 1,404 attributes from two wide-angle images. Sampling of 80% on collection and 84% on annotation returned pass rates of 98% and 97% respectively, for a 99.8% customer pass rate — all delivered in under one month. Aapya's dataset now models 300+ liquor products at 90–95% detection accuracy, positioning the platform to scale locally, regionally, and nationally.

data.items:
Photos of aisle segments plus matching individual bottle barcodes
Up to eight attributes provided per bottle
Polygon segmentation for bottles, bounding boxes for barcodes
Three-coordinate workflow removes duplicate attribute entry
Script-based YOLOv8 export built for the client's pipeline

data.title: Query & Response Evaluation and Ranking for Generative AI Chatbot

items.heading: Overview
items.text: Our client, an international technology company, was looking for a partner to assist in training its AI-enabled large language model (LLM) in both the relevance and accuracy of prompt query and response interactions. The project had a variety of goals, including:

data.items:
Query Evaluation: confirming the query is answerable.
Response Evaluation: confirming the response is correct, understandable, and complete.
Response Ranking: confirming the response is both natural and relevant based on the query.

items.text: In order to accomplish this, our client needed a partner with the ability to train the model with a variety of queries, paired with multiple responses based on our client’s requirements, all while sourcing a group of qualified contributors who could accurately analyze the data in detail and then categorize and rank it accordingly.

After understanding our client’s specific requirements, the DataForce team began building an offshore team, leveraging our global network that had the flexibility to add contributors as the project continued to grow. Prior to onboarding, applicants were screened to ensure they could review and answer prompts from the perspective of someone living in the United States.
Once applicants were approved and onboarded, they were given detailed instructions and training material on how to evaluate and rank queries and responses from the chatbot.
Building an evaluation and ranking process with quality assurance in mind:

data.items:
Each query and response was evaluated and ranked twice in efforts to find agreement and yield the highest-quality data.
If the annotators had opposing opinions, a third annotator was brought in to be the tie-breaker.

items.text: With this approach set as a standard in the early stages of the project, our client was able to leverage much-needed insights as the annotation team uncovered what did and did not make sense in the variety of queries and responses. For example, an answer could make sense but not be specific and measurable. This real-time feedback from the disagreement rate would reveal that the posed question is too difficult to get into an agreeable state. As the project continued, our client was able to refine project requirements by leveraging the opinions and findings from the annotation team.

Following the initial pilot, our client was very pleased with the progression of the model training and added multiple additional batches of data to be evaluated and ranked. Our client was able to constantly change project requirements based on the real-time feedback all while meeting the agreed-upon timeline. DataForce was able to provide responses with a high-quality output so our client could utilize the data collected as a valuable asset in training its generative AI chatbot model.

items.heading: The Challenge
items.text: Our client, a long-standing partner in the automotive industry, sought to train their autonomous driving algorithms to accurately identify various objects and elements at traffic intersections. The objectives ranged from recognizing simple objects, such as crosswalks and traffic lights, to interpreting more complex elements, like lane accessibility relative to a vehicle. The project presented unique challenges, including objects barely visible at a distance, which caused difficulties due to overlapping and perspective distortions, as well as undefined annotation cases for elements like roundabouts and bicycle lanes. Additionally, maintaining accuracy across a large volume of complex annotations required robust guidelines and processes.

items.heading: The Solution
items.text: The DataForce team leveraged its proprietary platform and introduced several innovative approaches to ensure efficiency and accuracy:

items.heading: The Results
items.bullets:
DataForce met and exceeded the client’s stringent requirements:
98% Accuracy: Ensured minimal rejections and high-quality data delivery.
Increased Volume: Delivered over double the expected volume of simple objects while achieving complex object targets within 21% of the originally projected image count.
Budget Efficiency: Streamlined processes allowed the team to meet these goals while staying within budget, prompting the client to expand object counts and adjust scope ratios.
Thanks to DataForce’s advanced annotations and efficient workflows, the client was able to enhance their algorithms and achieve faster development timelines, ultimately advancing their ability to navigate complex traffic scenarios.

items.heading: 1. Training and Onboarding
items.bullets:
Annotators underwent detailed training sessions via video calls, with demonstrations, examples, and clear guidelines.
Sessions were followed by a test to verify understanding before gaining access to production annotation tasks.

items.heading: 2. Workflow Optimization
items.bullets:
Tasks were segmented into Simple Experts for straightforward objects, and Complex Experts for advanced annotations, ensuring efficiency and focus.
Images were grouped by context and assigned to consistent pairs of annotators, preserving accuracy.
Workflow restrictors prevented task overload, ensuring fair distribution of work and reducing idle time across the team.

items.heading: 3. Scripting
items.bullets: Scripts were developed and integrated in the data pipeline, generating color-coded images, streamlining annotation workflows and enhancing quality.

items.heading: 4. Multi-Tiered Quality Assurance
items.bullets: A three-stage quality review process was established, including first- and second-level reviews, final annotation reviews, and internal expert assessments. This ensured precision and high-quality data transitions between teams.

items.heading: 5. Client Scope Alignment
items.bullets: Collaboration with the client clarified ambiguous cases and refined guidelines for consistent application.

data.title: Safety Text Translation at Scale for AI Content Moderation
data.short: Safety Text Translation at Scale for AI Content Moderation

items.heading: The Challenge
items.text: A global technology company was developing AI-powered content moderation tools designed to detect abusive and harmful online content. To support this initiative, the client needed to localize and post-edit large volumes of safety-related text, including messages, emails, and notifications across multiple languages. Although the content had already been machine-translated, human post-editing was required to ensure contextual accuracy, cultural relevance, and appropriate local tone. The output would be used to train AI models, making linguistic precision and consistency critical.

items.heading: The Solution
items.text:
DataForce implemented a localization and MTPE workflow purpose-built for safety text and AI training data. A global team of 80 specialized linguists was rapidly mobilized to support 12 language pairs, spanning both European and Asian markets. Content was divided into structured batches and assigned based on linguist expertise, availability, and proven performance, helping maintain quality while meeting tight deadlines. Quality management was embedded throughout the production process rather than treated as a separate step. Linguists received thorough onboarding and clear, client-specific guidelines focused on sensitive content handling, cultural nuance, and tone. These instructions were continuously refined between batches based on project manager feedback and prior learnings, enabling ongoing improvements in consistency and accuracy.
Project managers conducted regular quality checks with particular attention to local adaptation, such as: • Correct localization of personal names and cultural references (e.g., John → João, White House → Assembleia da República) • Tone appropriateness for safety and moderation use cases • Linguistic consistency across batches and contributors To support efficient execution, DataForce's technology team developed a custom technical workflow. Client-provided CSV files were pre-flighted and converted into bilingual review formats, allowing linguists to view source and target text side by side. This approach reduced friction, minimized errors, and enabled linguists to work at speed without compromising accuracy. Throughout the engagement, project managers, linguists, and the technical team worked in close coordination to ensure seamless delivery at scale.

items.heading: The Result
items.text: DataForce delivered high-quality, culturally accurate safety text localization at exceptional speed. Over the course of the project, 839,484 words were completed across multiple large batches.

Managing highly sensitive and potentially offensive content that required experienced linguists

Addressing technical complexity, as all content was delivered in CSV files that were not immediately ready for bilingual review

items.heading: Project Kickoff
items.bullets:
Project Decomposition: align on guidelines and match annotators accordingly
Annotator Exam: establish grading criteria prior to entering the project

items.heading: Sourcing
items.text: With a team of over 50 sourcing experts around the globe, we find and engage annotators with the right base-level requirements, then build an annotator profile to allow our sourcing teams to best match existing community members to the role, or to advertise and attract new community members.

items.heading: Qualification
items.text: Once potential annotators have been identified, DataForce evaluates their ability to complete human evaluation tasks both in general and specific to customer requirements. Annotators are tested on standard tasks and then on customer-specific tasks, where they are evaluated based on customer guidelines. These tests are randomized and chosen from a larger pool of tasks to maintain a high standard during qualification. We also have some specific language tests that validate the annotators' language capabilities.

items.heading: Training
items.text: Training, as an initial and ongoing process, is essential for sustained quality throughout the annotator lifecycle. It increases performance, builds rating consistency, and reassures annotators that they are being supported every step of the way. Our quality team is responsible for designing and implementing training at a program, locale, task, and annotator level. These trainings can be online interactive modules, self-study courses, live webinars, and direct feedback on annotator-specific content identified through regular quality processes.

items.heading: New Annotator Audit
items.text: During the initial phase of work on a project, the annotator will have spot-checks or audits completed to ensure they have understood the assignment and can apply the skills required to complete the tasks to a high standard.

items.heading: Quality Process and Metrics for Quality Control Oversight
items.text: Managing and controlling any annotator-based rating program means looking at both the quantitative and qualitative aspects of performance. While the data generated from our annotation gives a very quantitative view of an annotator's performance (tasks complete, timings, quality scores, etc.), data generated through our community interactions, training and quality webinars, and annotator support forums give us qualitative data on their engagement and performance levels. Our team continuously monitors annotator output. When areas are identified where performance is deviating from agreed KPIs, DataForce can provide additional training or support to ensure that the annotators are actively learning and improving as their tenure on the project progresses.

items.heading: Quality Monitoring, Controlling Processes, and Ongoing Quality Measures – KPIs
items.text: Outlier activities can often point to annotators who are not performing up to standard, or can give our quality team a mechanism to focus on whose work to review.

items.heading: Speed Tests
items.text: What is each annotator's average speed of completion versus the average speed of the total pool? This is run automatically as a background check and flags any annotator going faster by a determined amount compared to the average (depending on the number of tasks being reviewed, mean or median values may be used).

items.heading: Patterns
items.text: When looking at how an annotator rates tasks, do they consistently rate one option? For example, on a scale of 1 to 5, do they choose 3 a high percentage of the time compared to the pool? Do they rate consistently more negatively or positively than others?

items.heading: Spamsets
items.text: These are like the gold set test but much simpler. Spamsets are usually very basic questions that are designed to check that the annotator is concentrating.

items.heading: Consensus / Overlap
items.text: This automated task with human review looks at the consensus of each task and notes which annotators are in consensus out of the entire annotator pool. For example, Annotator A completed 100 tasks and agreed with the consensus 95% of the time, whereas Annotator B completed 100 tasks but agreed with the consensus only 50% of the time. This is not a measure of correctness but whether an annotator is in agreement with the other annotators as a group.

items.heading: Gold Set or Honeypot Testing
items.text: These comprise tasks with known answers that are injected into the normal task process (an annotator is not aware that the tasks are gold set tasks). Each annotator on the project receives the same set of tasks, and they can be ranked based on their answers. For example, Annotator A answered 19 out of 20 gold set questions correctly, whereas Annotator B answered 15 out of 20 gold set questions correctly. When creating gold sets, you can use a mixture of clear and ambiguous questions, allowing for a range of answers to the ambiguous questions in the scoring. Some tasks may need human review if, for example, there are divergent ratings on the task from the expected. This may be a result of unclear or misunderstood guidelines, or it can sometimes be timing-related.

items.heading: Spot Checks
items.text: This is the most manual task and usually requires a human quality controller with experience in the task to review an annotators work. These spot checks can be routine or instigated from an annotator being flagged on one or more of the outlier checks or from a low result on a gold set. Usually, a random set of the annotator's tasks are reviewed, and a decision is made on what action is required.

items.heading: Community Engagement
items.text: Our Community Engagement Team is continually in touch with our annotators, making sure feedback is continuously collected and addressed, preparing webinars for new community members, doing active social media listening, and managing DataForce social media channels.

data.title: Accelerating Specialized AI with Expert-Verified STEM Datasets

items.heading: The Challenge
items.text: Our enterprise client, a leader in AI research, faced the critical constraint limiting all specialized LLMs: a lack of high-quality, expert-verified training and validation data. They required a large-scale dataset to strengthen their model's reasoning capabilities across mathematics, physics, and chemistry, spanning educational levels from high school (K-12) through PhD.
items.bullets:
Scientific Depth: Problems and solutions had to be scientifically accurate and robust across all levels, particularly the complex logic required at the graduate level.
Topical Diversity: Minimal repetition and broad coverage of niche subtopics across all three domains.
Benchmarking Rigor: For the high school dataset, the client required a validated benchmark that included multi-LLM solution comparisons and a five-person blind expert annotation process covering solution accuracy, completeness, and step-by-step reasoning detail.

items.heading: The Solution
items.text: The DataForce team designed a customized, end-to-end workflow to ensure high volumes of verifiable content at scale.
items.bullets:
Streamlined Expert Qualification: Rapidly assembled a global cohort of PhD SMEs and specialized educators who passed a five-stage vetting pipeline, ensuring accuracy at the K-12 level and advanced conceptual rigor at the PhD level.
Empowered Creation and Diversity: Experts were given the flexibility to explore niche areas within their domains, increasing topical diversity and minimizing repetition.
Technology-Enabled Consistency and QA: The DataForce proprietary platform was configured with a specialized submission schema to enforce consistency in the Question → Step-by-Step Solution → Final Answer structure. The workflow included a multi-tier QA process, leveraging AI-assisted checks for consistency, followed by the mandatory human-in-the-Loop (HITL) review by QA specialists.
Advanced Benchmarking Infrastructure: To manage the five-person blind annotation requirement, the proprietary platform was configured with specialized dashboards, including an agreement matrix to track inter-rater reliability, assess performance, and provide the client with audit-ready insights into the benchmarking process.

items.heading: The Result
items.text: DataForce successfully embedded human intelligence directly into the client's AI training pipeline, accelerating domain-specific model performance beyond what internal R&D timelines would have allowed.

Thousands of high-quality STEM problems across mathematics, chemistry, and physics (high school through PhD)
Fully audited, five-person expert-annotated benchmark dataset, enabling precise comparison against competitor LLMs
Immediate project expansion, with the client replicating the workflow in a new complex domain: coding

items.heading: The Challenge
items.text: Our client, a global mobile game developer and publisher, was preparing to launch a newly localized version of their game but needed help deciding between the existing and updated localizations for Korean and Japanese markets. To best resonate with each audience, their research team aimed to evaluate the first-time user experience for role-playing game (RPG) newcomers in both regions. Specifically, the team was seeking feedback rooted in cultural understanding—requesting native-language insights from local users along with strategic oversight from an experienced global partner. They chose TransPerfect Games for our proven success supporting gaming companies across diverse markets and our unique combination of global leadership and local execution.

items.heading: The Solution
items.bullets:
TransPerfect Games delivered a tailored user research program with on-the-ground teams in both Korea and Japan. Leveraging our extensive database of verified players, we filtered candidates to match the client’s target audience. Ten qualified participants were selected from each country to:
• Play the game for 30 minutes while screen activity was recorded
• Participate in a moderated post-gameplay interview in their native language
This approach ensured that feedback captured both immediate player reactions and deeper cultural context—critical for accurately evaluating user engagement and preferences.

items.heading: The Results
items.bullets:
All gameplay recordings and interview data were collected and reviewed. Our in-house user research consultant then analyzed the aggregated data to identify key patterns, emotional responses, and friction points across both markets.
Thanks to TransPerfect Games’ cross-market leadership and local experts, the client gained insights and first-hand feedback that empowered them to confidently select the optimal localized version for launch, basing their decision on a data-driven strategy.

data.title: The final deliverable included a comprehensive report outlining

Which localized version players preferred and why
Gameplay elements that enhanced or detracted from the experience
Actionable recommendations for launch strategy

data.title: Global Game Localization: Empowering Fatshark's Warhammer Titles

items.heading: The Challenge
items.text: Fatshark, the acclaimed developer behind the Warhammer series, sought to bring its popular titles— Warhammer: Darktide and Warhammer: Vermintide 2— to a global audience. To achieve maximum reach and inclusivity, Fatshark required high-quality localization of Vermintide 2 into eight languages and Darktide into nine languages. Both games are set in the rich Warhammer universe, where terminology posed one of the most complex challenges. As a long-established world with vocabulary dating back to the late 1980s, Warhammer's lore contains countless unique and historically rooted terms. Maintaining consistency and accuracy required familiarity not only with the project but also with decades of established lore. This created a unique linguistic challenge, demanding careful management of established names, concepts, and in-game language to preserve authenticity and ensure an immersive experience for each target market.

items.heading: The Solution
items.text: With proven expertise in gaming localization, TransPerfect Games assembled a specialized team of more than 100 linguists fluent in each target language. The project involved:
items.bullets:
Coordinated project management to ensure smooth scheduling and communication with Fatshark
Consistent use of localization best practices, quality assurance, and in-game context review to maintain narrative integrity
Close collaboration with Fatshark to enable prompt feedback and seamless integration of localized content

items.heading: The Result
items.text: Both Darktide and Vermintide 2 were localized into all required languages and delivered on schedule, meeting Fatshark's high quality standards across 2.6 million translated words. The games launched successfully and became accessible to millions of new players worldwide, expanding Fatshark's fan base and strengthening its position in key global markets.

data.quote: Transperfect Games always nails it as our localisation partner for our award-winning Warhammer titles, Vermintide 2 and Darktide. They're key to making sure players everywhere get an authentic experience, even with our hectic release schedule and all the challenges being an AA studio which punches above their weight brings!

items.heading: The Client
items.text: An Am Law 10 law firm representing a global entertainment company that received a second request from the US Department of Justice (DOJ) regarding a $60 billion acquisition.

items.heading: The Challenges
items.text: Our client faced two major obstacles. First, more than 30 terabytes of data were collected in response to the second request – with only 60 days to complete collection, processing, review and production. Second, the firm’s cloud-based backup system created frequent snapshots of data (every four hours), resulting in an unusually high volume of duplicative files.

items.heading: The Solution
items.text: TransPerfect Legal worked in close collaboration with outside counsel and the client to design and execute a highly customised, defensible workflow consisting of three key components:

items.heading: The Results
items.bullets:
98%+ reduction in data volume from 30+ TB to 410 GB
85% of documents coded using TAR
222,000 documents identified for production
60-DAY second request deadline met with DOJ approval
Significant savings through defensible filtering and automation

items.heading: Forensic Deduplication Prior to Ingestion
items.text: To avoid the cost and delay of ingesting 30+ TBs of largely duplicative data, our forensic consultants applied pre-ingestion filters, including directory and file-level deduplication. This reduced the dataset to under 650 GB for ingestion into the processing phase.

items.heading: Application of Pre-Review Analytics®
items.text: We deployed our proprietary Digital Reef platform to further deduplicate, de-NIST and date-filter the dataset – including container files like PSTs and archives. Working closely with outside counsel, our team secured DOJ approval to apply Pre-Review Analytics®, which uses AI and metadata-driven filtering to isolate and exclude non-responsive content (e.g., irrelevant domains, file types and directories). This step reduced the volume to approximately 410 GB, or 1.5 million documents.

items.heading: Negotiation and Implementation of TAR
items.text: Finally, TransPerfect Legal and counsel negotiated TAR protocols with the DOJ’s antitrust team. Using Brainspace’s logistic regression-based TAR, a subject-matter expert reviewed 5,040 control documents and 1,750 training documents. Once agreed-upon recall and precision thresholds were reached, 85% of the population was coded. The DOJ approved the process after validating a random sample of non-responsive documents.

items.heading: The Client
items.text: A global manufacturer facing a high-stakes class action lawsuit related to alleged product defects.

items.heading: The Challenges
items.bullets:
As part of early discovery efforts, the client collected more than 8.4 million documents (8,462,117) for potential review. After applying standard culling techniques – including duplicate detection, deNISTing, keyword searches and basic filtering – the dataset was reduced by 80.5%. Still, over 1.6 million documents (1,651,094) remained in the review population.
Reviewing that volume would have placed a significant burden on time and cost. At a rate of 50 documents per hour and $42/hour for contract reviewers, the projected review cost exceeded $1.1 million. A 20-person review team working 10-hour days would have needed 138 business days to complete the task – far too long for the legal team’s timeline.

items.heading: The Solution
items.bullets:
To accelerate the process and reduce costs, the client engaged TransPerfect Legal. Our team deployed Digital Reef’s Pre-Review Analytics to run a second layer of culling – this time using intelligent pattern recognition and relevance modelling.
That additional pass removed 1,387,350 more documents, pushing the overall reduction rate to 96.4% and leaving just 263,744 documents for final review. By dramatically reducing review volume while maintaining defensibility, TransPerfect Legal helped the client contain costs, accelerate discovery, and stay focused on the broader litigation strategy.

items.heading: Processing & Filtering
